pages.title: Debug a BEC server service in VS Code
headings: Debug a BEC server service in VS Code
Step 1: identify the service you want to debug
Step 2: stop the already running copy of that service
Step 3: open the service entry file
Step 5: start the service from VS Code

sections.heading: Debug a BEC server service in VS Code
sections.text:
If you want to debug a BEC service with breakpoints, VS Code is usually the easiest option.
The basic idea is:
keep the rest of BEC running normally
stop only the service you want to inspect
launch that service from VS Code
reproduce the problem from a client
This gives you breakpoints, variable inspection, stack traces, and a regular terminal for logs.

sections.heading: When this is useful
sections.text:
This workflow is helpful when:
logs are not enough to explain the problem
you want to inspect object state during execution
a service is taking an unexpected code path
you want to step through request handling callback by callback

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.text:
You will usually need:
the BEC repository open in VS Code
the correct Python environment selected in VS Code
the same BEC config that the rest of your running services use
a running Redis server and the rest of the BEC stack
If you normally start the stack with:
bec-server start
then the services are usually running in tmux. You can inspect them with:
bec-server attach

sections.heading: Step 1: identify the service you want to debug
sections.text:
Typical services are:
bec-scan-server
bec-device-server
bec-file-writer
bec-scihub
bec-scan-bundler
Examples:
queueing and scan execution issues: bec-scan-server
motion, device communication, RPC issues: bec-device-server
file writing issues: bec-file-writer

sections.heading: Step 2: stop the already running copy of that service
sections.text:
This is important. BEC services are unique services, so you generally should not run a second copy of the same one while the original is still active.
If the stack is running in tmux:
run bec-server attach
move to the pane of the target service
stop it with Ctrl+C
leave the other services running
Now VS Code can launch that service instead.

sections.heading: Step 3: open the service entry file
sections.text:
In the BEC repository, the service entry points are the CLI launch files:
bec_server/bec_server/scan_server/cli/launch.py
bec_server/bec_server/device_server/cli/launch.py
bec_server/bec_server/file_writer/cli/launch.py
bec_server/bec_server/scihub/cli/launch.py
Open the one that matches the service you want to debug.

sections.heading: Step 4: add breakpoints
sections.text:
Set breakpoints in the code path you want to inspect.
Good first breakpoint locations are often:
the main() function in the service launch.py
the callback or handler that receives the request
the method where you suspect state becomes wrong
If you are not yet sure where the issue is, start near the service entry point and move deeper once you see the flow.

sections.heading: Step 5: start the service from VS Code
sections.text:
The sibling BEC repository already contains a basic VS Code Python launch configuration for debugging the current file.
That means a simple workflow is:
open the correct launch.py
select the VS Code Run and Debug view
choose Python: Debug current file
start debugging
If you need command-line arguments such as --config, add them in the VS Code debug configuration before launching.
For example, the service should receive the same config file you would use from the terminal:
--config path/to/your_config.yaml
You can also pass a Redis address directly:
--bec-server localhost:6379

sections.heading: Step 6: reproduce the problem
sections.text:
Once the service is running under the debugger:
start the scan, move, or workflow from your BEC client
let execution hit your breakpoints
inspect variables, object attributes, and the call stack
step over or into the next methods as needed
This is usually the clearest way to answer questions like:
what request actually arrived here?
what metadata did this service receive?
why did this branch execute?
what internal state changed just before the failure?

sections.heading: Logs still help
sections.text:
Even when you are using breakpoints, logs are still useful.
If you want more terminal output from the service, pass a more verbose log level in the debug arguments:
--log-level DEBUG
or, if really necessary:
--log-level TRACE
DEBUG is usually a better first choice than TRACE, because TRACE can become noisy quickly.
You can also use:
bec-log-monitor --filter "scan_server"
or another suitable filter string in a separate terminal.

sections.heading: A minimal VS Code workflow
sections.text:
For most cases, this is enough:
start BEC normally with bec-server start
attach with bec-server attach
stop only the target service
open its launch.py in VS Code
add breakpoints
start Python: Debug current file
pass the same config arguments as the normal service
reproduce the issue from the client

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.text:
Forgetting to stop the original service before starting the VS Code one.
Running the service with a different config from the rest of the stack.
Using the wrong Python interpreter in VS Code.
Putting breakpoints too deep before first confirming the request path.
Turning on TRACE immediately and making the output harder to read.

pages.title: Install BEC Locally
headings: Create and activate a Python environment

sections.heading: Install BEC Locally
sections.text:
Overview
Install BEC in a local Python environment, start the required services, and open a working BEC client session on
your own machine.

sections.heading: Prerequisites
sections.text:
You have Python 3.11 or newer available.
You can install Python packages in a virtual environment or Conda environment.
You can install and run redis-server.
You can install and use tmux.
You have network access to the repositories you want to install from.

sections.heading: Create and activate a Python environment
Install the BEC packages
sections.text:
Make sure your Python environment is active before installing anything.
Choose the installation style that matches your goal.
/// tab Standard install
Use this if you want a working local BEC environment and do not need to edit the source code directly.
pip install bec_lib
pip install bec_ipython_client
pip install bec_server
pip install ophyd_devices
If you also want the widget and GUI stack:
pip install bec_widgets
///
/// tab Editable developer install
Use this if you want to work on the BEC source code, add devices, or develop widgets locally.
Clone the repositories you need:
git clone https://github.com/bec-project/ophyd_devices.git
git clone https://github.com/bec-project/bec.git
git clone https://github.com/bec-project/bec_widgets.git
Then install the packages in editable mode:
pip install -e './bec/bec_lib[dev]'
pip install -e './bec/bec_ipython_client[dev]'
pip install -e './bec/bec_server[dev]'
pip install -e './ophyd_devices[dev]'
If you also want widget development tools:
pip install -e './bec_widgets[dev]'
///

sections.heading: Install and start Redis
sections.text:
BEC requires a running Redis server for message transport and shared runtime state.
/// tab Conda
conda install redis-server tmux
redis-server
///
/// tab macOS
brew install redis
brew install tmux
redis-server
///
By default, Redis starts on port 6379.
tip
Redis writes a dump.rdb file in the directory where it is started. Run it in a location with enough available
disk space.

sections.heading: Start the BEC service stack
sections.text:
Open a terminal where the same Python environment is active and start the BEC services:
bec-server start
This typically launches the BEC services inside tmux.
If you want to inspect the running services:
bec-server attach
Detach from the tmux session again with Ctrl+b d.

sections.heading: Start the client
sections.text:
Open a new terminal, activate the same Python environment, and start the BEC client:
bec
If you only want the terminal client and not the GUI:
bec --nogui
When startup succeeds, the prompt changes to the BEC prompt and you can run commands such as:
dev.show_all()

sections.heading: Continue with your local session
sections.text:
At this point, BEC is running locally and ready for you.
Congratulations!
You have successfully installed BEC locally and started a working client session.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.text:
Installing the Python packages without first activating the intended environment.
Starting the client before redis-server or the BEC services are running.

sections.heading: Next Steps
sections.text:
Continue with Open BEC if you want the full startup context.
Continue with Load your first config to begin working in the local session.

pages.title: Send a custom notification event
headings: Route the event to a messaging service

sections.heading: Send a custom notification event
sections.text:
Overview
Publish a custom notification event from BEC code so it can be routed to messaging services such as SciLog, Signal, or Teams.

sections.heading: Prerequisites
sections.text:
You are working in custom BEC code such as a plugin, service extension, or beamline-specific helper.
Your code has access to a BEC connector, for example self.connector or client.connector.
The target messaging service is enabled for your deployment or session.
If you want the event to be forwarded automatically, you have configured a matching route in Set Up Auto Notifications{ data-preview }.

sections.heading: Notification publish interface
sections.text:
Publish a notification with:
connector.notify(event, message)
event is a string such as "beamline_ready" or "sample_mount_failed"
message can be either a plain string or a NotificationMessageObject

sections.heading: Send a simple custom event
sections.text:
If plain text is enough, send the event name together with a string message:
self.connector.notify(
"beamline_ready",
"Beamline checks passed and the station is ready for users.",
)
BEC wraps the string into a notification message object automatically before routing it.

sections.heading: Send a richer custom event
sections.text:
Use NotificationMessageObject when you want formatted text, tags, or attachments that can be adapted to the target messaging service:
from bec_lib.messaging_services import NotificationMessageObject
msg = NotificationMessageObject()
msg.add_text("Sample mount failed", bold=True, color="red")
msg.add_text(" Please check the robot status before retrying.")
msg.add_tags(["sample-exchange", "robot"])
self.connector.notify("sample_mount_failed", msg)
This is useful when the same event should later be routed to services with richer formatting support, especially SciLog.

sections.heading: Route the event to a messaging service
sections.text:
Publishing a custom event does not send it anywhere by itself. To forward it automatically, configure a route for the same event name from the BEC client as described in Set Up Auto Notifications{ data-preview }:
bec.messaging.scilog.set_auto_notifications(
"beamline_ready",
enabled=True,
scopes="default",
)
After that, every beamline_ready notification published by your code is forwarded to the configured SciLog scope.

sections.heading: Use a stable event name
sections.text:
Choose one event string and keep it consistent between the publisher and the routing configuration:
self.connector.notify("sample_mount_failed", "Robot reported a mount failure.")
bec.messaging.signal.set_auto_notifications(
"sample_mount_failed",
enabled=True,
scopes="beamline-ops",
)
If the event names do not match exactly, BEC will not route the notification.
Congratulations!
You can now publish custom notification events from BEC code and connect them to the automatic notification routing system.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.text:
connector.notify(...) only publishes the event. It does not automatically choose a messaging service unless you configured a matching route.
The event name in notify(...) and the event name in set_auto_notifications(...) must match exactly.
Use NotificationMessageObject when you need tags, formatting, or attachments. Use a plain string when a simple text notification is enough.

pages.title: Send messages to SciLog
headings: Create and send a simple message
Log device positions as a table

sections.heading: Send messages to SciLog
sections.text:
Overview
Send text, tags, and attachments from the BEC IPython client to a configured SciLog messaging service.

sections.heading: Prerequisites
sections.text:
You have a running BEC IPython client session.
SciLog messaging is enabled for your deployment or session.
Logbook selection
BEC automatically configures SciLog to use the logbook associated with the currently active pgroup.

sections.heading: Create and send a simple message
sections.text:
Create a new SciLog message object from the BEC client and send it:
msg = bec.messaging.scilog.new()
msg.add_text("Beamline is ready for alignment.")
msg.send()
You can also create and send a short message in one line:
bec.messaging.scilog.new("Beamline checks completed.").send()

sections.heading: Add formatting and tags
sections.text:
SciLog messages support formatted text and tags:
msg = bec.messaging.scilog.new()
msg.add_text("Alignment warning", bold=True, color="yellow")
msg.add_text(" Check the slit positions before continuing.")
msg.add_tags(["alignment", "warning"])
msg.send()
add_text() supports:
bold=True
italic=True
color="red", "green", "yellow", "pink", "blue" or "black"
Pen Colors vs Markers
In SciLog, black, red, and green are pen colors. yellow, pink, and blue are markers.
BEC adds the default bec tag automatically if you do not provide tags yourself.
If you want to change the default tags for the current client session, set them explicitly:
bec.messaging.scilog.set_default_tags(["bec", "beamline-x", "commissioning"])

sections.heading: Attach a file
sections.text:
Add attachments from a local path before sending the message:
msg = bec.messaging.scilog.new("Attached: latest detector snapshot.")
msg.add_attachment("/path/to/snapshot.png")
msg.send()
For image attachments, you can also provide display dimensions:
msg = bec.messaging.scilog.new("Overview image")
msg.add_attachment("/path/to/overview.png", width=800, height=450)
msg.send()
Attachments must exist on disk and must be smaller than 5 MB.

sections.heading: Combine text, tags, and attachments
sections.text:
SciLog messages are built from ordered elements. BEC keeps the order in which you add content, so you can structure a message as text, image, text or in any other sequence that fits your note.
In practice, you will often send all parts together:
msg = bec.messaging.scilog.new()
msg.add_text("Beam position before correction:")
msg.add_attachment("/path/to/before.png", width=700)
msg.add_text("Beam position after correction:")
msg.add_attachment("/path/to/after.png", width=700)
msg.send()
You can also combine formatted text, tags, and attachments in one message:
msg = bec.messaging.scilog.new()
msg.add_text("Scan quality check failed.", bold=True, color="red")
msg.add_text(" See the attached plot for details.")
msg.add_tags(["quality-check", "scan"])
msg.add_attachment("/path/to/scan_summary.pdf")
msg.send()

sections.heading: Use SciLog wrapper helpers
sections.text: BEC also provides wrapper methods for common SciLog use cases. These are convenient when you want to send structured content directly without building the message element by element.

sections.heading: Log device positions as a table
sections.text:
Use log_positions() to capture the current state of devices in SciLog. It collects the same kind of position information you would inspect with dev.wm(...) and sends it as a formatted table.
For example, log all sample-positioning devices that match a wildcard:
bec.messaging.scilog.log_positions(
devices="sam*",
title="Current sample positions",
tags="snapshot",
)
This creates a SciLog entry with columns for:
device
readback
setpoint
limits
You can also pass other device selections accepted by dev.wm(...), for example a list of device names or device objects.

sections.heading: Log source code
sections.text:
Use log_code() to send source code to SciLog as a Python code block. This is useful for macros, helper functions, or other small snippets that should be recorded alongside a measurement.
Log the source of a function directly:
def align_sample():
samx.set(1.2)
samy.set(-0.4)
bec.messaging.scilog.log_code(
align_sample,
title="Alignment macro used for this run",
tags="code",
)
Congratulations!
You can now send SciLog messages from the BEC IPython client, log device positions and source code, add tags, and attach files when needed.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.text:
bec.messaging.scilog.new() raises an error if SciLog messaging is not enabled for the current deployment or session.
add_attachment(...) fails if the file does not exist or is larger than 5 MB.
Default tags are added automatically. If you call set_default_tags(...), those tags are used for later messages in the current client session.

pages.title: Send messages to Signal
headings: Create and send a simple message

sections.heading: Send messages to Signal
sections.text:
Overview
Send direct Signal messages from the BEC IPython client by addressing recipients with their phone numbers.

sections.heading: Prerequisites
sections.text:
You have a running BEC IPython client session.
Signal messaging is enabled for your deployment or session.
Private phone numbers
Make sure to not commit source code with your private phone number to version control. If you want to share code that includes phone numbers, consider using environment variables or configuration files to keep the numbers private.

sections.heading: Create and send a simple message
sections.text:
Create a new Signal message object from the BEC client and send it to a phone number:
msg = bec.messaging.signal.new()
msg.add_text("Beamline is ready for alignment.")
msg.send(scope="+41791234567")
You can also create and send a short message in one line:
bec.messaging.signal.new("Beamline checks completed.").send(scope="+41791234567")

sections.heading: Send to phone numbers directly
sections.text:
For Signal, pass the recipient phone number to send(scope=...).
msg = bec.messaging.signal.new("Scan finished successfully.")
msg.send(scope="+41791234567")
BEC normalizes valid phone numbers before sending them to Signal.
For example, Swiss numbers such as 079 123 45 67 and 0041 79 123 45 67 are converted to +41791234567.
msg = bec.messaging.signal.new("Direct message using a local number.")
msg.send(scope="079 123 45 67")
Country codes required
BEC always normalizes valid phone numbers without country codes to use the Swiss country code +41 by default. If you want to send messages to phone numbers in other countries, make sure to include the correct country code in the recipient number.
You can also send the same message to more than one phone number:
msg = bec.messaging.signal.new("Please confirm detector status.")
msg.send(scope=["+41791234567", "+41795554433"])

sections.heading: Attach a file
sections.text:
Add attachments from a local path before sending the message:
msg = bec.messaging.signal.new("Attached: latest detector snapshot.")
msg.add_attachment("/path/to/snapshot.png")
msg.send(scope="+41791234567")
Attachments must exist on disk and must be smaller than 5 MB.
<!-- ## 4. Add a sticker
Signal messages can include stickers:
msg = bec.messaging.signal.new("Alignment completed.")
msg.add_sticker("sticker_123")
msg.send(scope="+41791234567")

sections.heading: Combine text and stickers
sections.text:
You can also mix text and stickers in one message:
msg = bec.messaging.signal.new()
msg.add_text("The scan queue is empty.")
msg.add_sticker("sticker_123")
msg.send(scope="+41791234567")
Congratulations!
You can now send direct Signal messages from the BEC IPython client, address recipients by phone number, and include attachments when needed.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.text:
bec.messaging.signal.new() raises an error if Signal messaging is not enabled for the current deployment or session.
send(scope=...) is where you provide the recipient phone number.
add_attachment(...) fails if the file does not exist or is larger than 5 MB.
Valid phone numbers are normalized automatically before sending.

pages.title: Set the Active Account with bec-set-account
headings: Set the Active Account with bec-set-account

sections.heading: Set the Active Account with bec-set-account
sections.text:
Overview
Set the active account for the BEC server using the local bec-set-account wrapper from the beamline config directory.
This is a PSI-specific guide. It assumes that you already know the correct process-group account, for example p12345.

sections.heading: Prerequisites
sections.text:
You are in the beamline config directory that contains the bec-set-account wrapper, for example /sls/x99sa/config/bec/production.
You have write access to the config directory and permission to change the active account, typically a PSI beamline scientist or staff member.
You know the process-group account you want to activate, for example p12345.
You are connected to the PSI or relevant beamline network.

sections.heading: Check that bec-set-account is available
sections.text:
In a terminal, run:
./bec-set-account --help
You should see help output similar to:
Usage: ./bec-set-account
Change the active pgroup in BEC to the specified pgroup.

sections.heading: Set the active account
sections.text:
On the beamline, the wrapper already knows how to update the BEC server account. You only need to specify the process-group account:
./bec-set-account p12345
The command sets the active account for the BEC server.

sections.heading: Verify the result
sections.text:
If the command succeeds, it prints a confirmation message similar to:
Account p12345 has been set successfully.
Congratulations!
You have successfully set the active account with bec-set-account.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.text:
Using a process-group value that does not match the required format p followed by exactly five digits.
Running the command outside the config directory that contains the wrapper.
Running the command on a machine that cannot reach the BEC server environment.

sections.heading: Set up auto notifications
sections.text:
Overview
Configure BEC to send automatic notifications for scan and alarm events through a messaging service such as SciLog or Signal.

sections.heading: Prerequisites
sections.text:
You have a running BEC IPython client session.
The messaging service you want to use is enabled for your deployment or session.
You know which target scope to use for that service, for example a SciLog logbook or a Signal group scope.

sections.heading: Notification interface and event types
sections.text:
Auto notifications are configured per messaging service from the BEC client with:
bec.messaging. .set_auto_notifications(event_type, enabled=True, scopes=...)
Supported event types are:
Event type
Emitted when
"new_scan"
A scan enters the open state, meaning BEC has started the scan.
"scan_completed"
A scan finishes with the status closed or user_completed .
"alarm_warning"
BEC raises an alarm with warning severity.
"alarm_minor"
BEC raises an alarm with minor severity.
"alarm_major"
BEC raises an alarm with major severity.
"scan_interlock"
The scan interlock is triggered because beamline states do not match, and again when that interlock is cleared.
Custom event names
You can also use custom event names. BEC supports any event string, as long as something in your deployment publishes notifications with the same event name.
To learn how to publish one of these events from custom BEC code, see Send a Custom Notification Event{ data-preview }.
For example, if a custom service or plugin publishes a beamline_ready notification, you can route it like this:
bec.messaging.scilog.set_auto_notifications(
"beamline_ready",
enabled=True,
scopes="default",
)

sections.heading: Enable an automatic notification
sections.text:
Enable a notification by choosing the service, event, and target scope.
For example, route new scan notifications to SciLog:
bec.messaging.scilog.set_auto_notifications(
"new_scan",
enabled=True,
scopes="default",
)
This stores a routing rule for the new_scan event. When a new scan starts, BEC forwards the notification to the configured SciLog scope.
You can do the same for Signal when your deployment exposes a named Signal scope:
bec.messaging.signal.set_auto_notifications(
"alarm_major",
enabled=True,
scopes="beamline-ops",
)

sections.heading: Add more event routes
sections.text:
You can enable more than one event for the same service:
bec.messaging.scilog.set_auto_notifications(
"scan_completed",
enabled=True,
scopes="default",
)
bec.messaging.scilog.set_auto_notifications(
"scan_interlock",
enabled=True,
scopes="default",
)
You can also route the same event to more than one service. For example, keep SciLog for the permanent record and send major alarms to Signal as well:
bec.messaging.scilog.set_auto_notifications(
"alarm_major",
enabled=True,
scopes="default",
)
bec.messaging.signal.set_auto_notifications(
"alarm_major",
enabled=True,
scopes="beamline-ops",
)

sections.heading: Use the default scope
sections.text:
If your messaging service already has a suitable default scope, set it once and omit scopes= afterwards:
bec.messaging.scilog.set_default_scope("default")
bec.messaging.scilog.set_auto_notifications(
"new_scan",
enabled=True,
)
This is useful when most notifications should go to the same logbook or group.

sections.heading: Disable an automatic notification
sections.text:
Disable a route by setting enabled=False for the same event and scope:
bec.messaging.scilog.set_auto_notifications(
"new_scan",
enabled=False,
scopes="default",
)
If that was the only route for this service and event, BEC removes it from the notification configuration.
Congratulations!
You have configured automatic notifications in BEC. You can now route scan and alarm events to your messaging services without sending each message manually.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.text:
set_auto_notifications(...) raises an error if the messaging service is not enabled for the current deployment or session.
Use the supported event strings exactly as shown above.
For services with configured scopes such as SciLog, the scope must exist before you enable auto notifications.
Signal auto notifications are typically routed to a configured Signal scope such as a group, not to an arbitrary phone number.

pages.title: Update BEC to the Latest Version
headings: Update BEC to the Latest Version

sections.heading: Update BEC to the Latest Version
sections.text:
Overview
This is a how-to guide on updating BEC to the latest version. This will re-install BEC and all its dependencies in a fresh environment.
Please note that this is a PSI-specific guide and will not be applicable to other installations of BEC. For other installations, please refer to the installation guide.

sections.heading: Prerequisites
sections.text:
You are a beamline scientist or are responsible for maintaining BEC at the beamline.
You are within the PSI intranet.
Important
Before updating BEC, please make sure that no data acquisition is currently running in BEC as the update process will require restarting BEC and all its services.

sections.heading: Updating BEC
sections.text:
The update process is built around Gitea pipelines. In the following example, we will show you the steps for x01da / Debye but the process is the same for all beamlines.
Go to the Gitea repository for your CPS deployments: https://gitea.psi.ch/cps-deployments
Find the your beamline's deployment repository. For x01da, it is https://gitea.psi.ch/cps-deployments/sls-x01da
Click on the "Actions" tab.
SelectAction
On the left side, select the bec_workflow.yaml workflow.
SelectWorkflow
On the right side, click on the "Run workflow" button.
RunWorkflow
In the workflow dialog, select the hosts you want to update BEC on.
SelectHosts
Host selection
**Option 1**: Update all hosts: You can simply update all hosts by using "bec" as host.
**Option 2**: Update only a specific host: If you only want to update a specific host, specify the full hostname, e.g. "x01da-bec-001.psi.ch".
Click on the "Run workflow" button to start the update process.
You can monitor the progress of the workflow in the "Actions" tab. Click on the currently running workflow to see the logs. The process will take around 5 to 10 minutes.
Congratulations!
You have successfully updated BEC to the latest version.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.text: If the workflow fails and cannot find the hostname, it is likely that there was a typo in the hostname or the ".psi.ch" part was missing. Make sure to specify the full hostname, e.g. "x01da-bec-001.psi.ch".

pages.title: Work with VS Code
headings: Open VS Code in the correct folder

sections.heading: Work with VS Code
sections.text:
Overview
This is a how-to guide on using VS Code for working with your BEC plugin.

sections.heading: Prerequisites
sections.text:
You have write access to your beamline plugin directory, for example /sls/ /config/bec/production/ .
If you don't have write access, you can still use VS Code to create and edit files outside of the deployment but you cannot modify the plugin repository directly.

sections.heading: Open VS Code in the correct folder
Install recommended extensions
sections.text:
When you open the deployment folder, VS Code will prompt you to install recommended extensions. We recommend installing them.
RecommendedExtensions
This will give you access to Python language support, formatters, linters but also H5Web for previewing HDF5 files.

sections.heading: Common Pitfalls
sections.text:
If Python syntax highlighting and auto-completion are not working, check that you have the Python extension installed and that the correct directory is open.
If you cannot edit files in the deployment, check that you have write access to the deployment directory. Experiment accounts usually do not have write access to the production deployment, so you may need to log in with your personal account.

sections.heading: Next Steps
sections.text:
Continue with Add Changes to Your Plugin if you
want to commit and push your changes.
Congratulations!
You have successfully set up VS Code for working with your BEC plugin.

pages.title: Add Changes to Your Plugin Repository
headings: Add Changes to Your Plugin Repository
Steps to add changes to your plugin repository

sections.heading: Add Changes to Your Plugin Repository
sections.text:
Overview
This is a how-to guide on how to add changes to your plugin repository. This will allow you to update your plugin with new features, bug fixes or config changes.
If you are familiar with Git, this How-To will be straightforward for you. If you are new to Git, don't worry, we will guide you through the process step by step.

sections.heading: Prerequisites
sections.text: You are a beamline scientist and have access to your plugin repository on /sls/ /config/bec, e.g. /sls/x01da/config/bec.

sections.heading: Steps to add changes to your plugin repository
sections.text:
First, locate the correct deployment directory.
Use:
/sls/ /config/bec/ /
where:
is the name of your beamline, e.g. x01da.
is the name of your deployment, e.g. production or test.
is the name of your plugin, e.g. x01da_bec.
Examples
Default production instance: /sls/x01da/config/bec/production/x01da_bec
Test deployment (if available): /sls/x01da/config/bec/test/x01da_bec
Change into the repository directory and check which files have changed.
cd /sls/x01da/config/bec/production/x01da_bec
git status
git status shows modified files, deleted files, and any new files that are not yet tracked by Git.
Edit the files you want to change, or add new files to the repository.
After you have made your changes, add them to Git, commit them, and push them to the remote repository.
/// tab Terminal
Stage changes to tracked files:
git add -u
If you created a new file, add it explicitly:
git add path/to/new-file
Check the result with:
git status
Commit your changes with a meaningful commit message, for example:
git commit -m "Update device configuration for the Eiger detector"
Push your changes:
git push
///
/// tab VS Code
Open the repository folder in VS Code.
Go to the **Source Control** view.
Review the changed files.
Files under **Changes** are modified tracked files.
Files under **Untracked Changes** are new files that still need to be added to Git.
Stage the files you want to include in the commit.
You can stage individual files with the + button, or stage all changes from the Source Control menu.
Enter a meaningful commit message in the message box and commit the changes.
Push the changes using **Sync Changes** or **Push** in the Source Control menu.
///
After pushing your changes, you can open the Gitea repository:
https://gitea.psi.ch/bec/
Then continue with Merge changes to main.

sections.heading: Next Steps
sections.text:
Continue with Merge changes to main to integrate your branch into the main branch.
Continue with Update BEC to the latest version to deploy the updated repository.
Congratulations!
You have successfully added your changes to the plugin repository. You can now deploy the updated repository to your BEC instance.

sections.heading: Merge Changes to main
sections.text:
Overview
This is a how-to guide on merging your changes into the main branch of your plugin repository.
Use this after you have committed and pushed your changes to a branch and you want to make them part of the main line of development.

sections.heading: Prerequisites
sections.text:
You have already pushed your changes to the remote repository.
You can access your repository in Gitea.
Your branch is ready to be reviewed and merged.

sections.heading: Steps to merge your changes
sections.text:
Open your repository in Gitea, for example:
https://gitea.psi.ch/bec/
Open the **Pull Requests** tab.
NewPullRequest
On the right, click on the **New Pull Request** button.
NewPullRequestButton
This will open the pull request creation page, where you can select the base and compare branches.
Select the base branch (left) as main and the compare branch as your feature branch (right).
SelectBranches
On the right, click the **New Pull Request** button to create the pull request.
CreatePullRequest
Add a title and description for your pull request, then click **Create Pull Request** again.
PullRequestDetails
Request a review from your team members.
It is always good practice to have at least one other person review your changes before merging.
Gitea allows you to request specific reviewers on the pull request page by adding them in the "Reviewers" section.
You can also add someone from the BEC team as a reviewer if you want feedback.
RequestReview
Review your changes carefully.
Make sure all checks pass.
Checks
If any checks fail, fix the issues in your branch and push the changes again. The pull request will update automatically. If you need help understanding or fixing failed checks, ask for help from your team or the BEC team.
If your branch is not up to date with main, you may need to update it before merging. You can do this by merging main into your branch or rebasing your branch onto main. After updating, push the changes to the remote repository. Gitea offers a button to update the branch if it is behind main.
UpdateBranch
Merge the pull request into main.
MergePullRequest
After the merge, Gitea may offer to delete the feature branch. This is usually fine if you no longer need it.

sections.heading: Common Pitfalls
sections.text:
If the pull request shows unexpected files, go back to your branch and check git status and git diff.
If Gitea reports merge conflicts, update your branch with the latest main, resolve the conflicts locally, and push again.
If the base branch is not main, double-check the target before merging.

sections.heading: Next Steps
sections.text:
Continue with Update BEC to the latest version to deploy the merged changes.
Congratulations!
You have successfully merged your changes into main. You can now deploy the updated repository to your BEC instance.

pages.title: Access History with a Waveform
headings: Plot the latest scan in a Waveform
Add a DAP curve to history data
Read data back from the Waveform

sections.heading: Access History with a Waveform
sections.text:
Goal
Plot data from a completed scan in a Waveform and know when to use bec.history directly.
Use bec.history when you want scan data as Python objects. Use a Waveform history curve when you want to inspect a
previous scan in the GUI or attach a DAP curve to it.
Live curves and history curves
A Waveform curve is a live device curve unless you pass scan_number or scan_id to wf.plot(...).
For example, wf.plot(device_x="samx", device_y="bpm4i") follows live BEC scan updates. If the Waveform does
not yet have a scan attached, it initializes from the current scan when one exists, or from the latest history
entry otherwise. This is useful for live plotting because the curve can show the most recently measured data and
then update with later scans. Use scan_number or scan_id when you want a fixed history curve that is not
replaced by live-scan updates.

sections.heading: Prerequisites
sections.text:
BEC is running with Terminal + Dock.
At least one completed scan is available through bec.history.
The history scan contains samx and bpm4i data.

sections.heading: Inspect the latest scan directly
sections.text:
Fetch the latest completed scan from BEC history:
scan = bec.history[-1]
Read the motor and signal arrays directly:
x = scan.devices.samx.samx.read()["value"]
y = scan.devices.bpm4i.bpm4i.read()["value"]
Use this path when you want to do Python analysis yourself, pass the data to another package, or inspect metadata:
scan.metadata["bec"]
For a fuller guide to direct history access, see
Access BEC History{ data-preview }.

sections.heading: Plot the latest scan in a Waveform
sections.text:
Create a Waveform:
wf = gui.bec.new(gui.available_widgets.Waveform)
Add a history curve for the latest scan:
wf.plot(
device_x="samx",
device_y="bpm4i",
scan_number=-1,
label="latest bpm4i history",
)
For scan_number, negative values behave like history list indices. -1 means the latest scan, -2 means the scan
before that. Positive values are resolved as BEC scan numbers.

sections.heading: Plot a specific scan ID
sections.text:
Use a scan ID when you want to refer to one exact scan:
scan = bec.history[-1]
scan_id = scan.metadata["bec"]["scan_id"]
wf.plot(
device_x="samx",
device_y="bpm4i",
scan_id=scan_id,
label=f"bpm4i {scan_id}",
)

sections.heading: Add a DAP curve to history data
sections.text:
History curves can be fitted by DAP in the same way as live or custom curves:
wf.plot(
device_x="samx",
device_y="bpm4i",
scan_number=-1,
label="latest bpm4i fit",
dap="GaussianModel",
)
Inspect the fit output:
wf.get_dap_summary()
wf.get_dap_params()

sections.heading: Use the GUI history browser
sections.text:
You can also add history curves from the Waveform GUI:
Open the Waveform scan history browser from the plot toolbar :material-manage-search:.
Select the scan, device, and signal you want to inspect.
Add the selected history signal to the Waveform.

sections.heading: Read data back from the Waveform
sections.text:
After plotting, retrieve the curve data from the Waveform:
data = wf.get_all_data()
The result is a dictionary keyed by curve label:
data["latest bpm4i history"]["x"]
data["latest bpm4i history"]["y"]
Result
You can inspect scan history directly through bec.history, plot it in a Waveform, fit history curves with DAP,
and retrieve plotted curve data with wf.get_all_data().

pages.title: Add a Widget to the GUI
headings: Add a Widget to the GUI
Add a widget to the dock
Add a dock and widget in one command
Add another dock next to it
Put multiple widgets in one dock

sections.heading: Add a Widget to the GUI
sections.text:
Overview
Add a BEC Widget to an existing Dock Area from the BEC IPython session, keep a reference to it, and place additional widgets next to it.
This guide starts from the same Terminal + Dock setup used in the quick-start tutorials. Use it when you already have BEC running and want to build or adjust a GUI from the command line.
If you want the introductory walkthrough first, start with Plot your first waveform{ data-preview } or Create Your First GUI{ data-preview }.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.text:
Start BEC with the Terminal + Dock interface.
Make sure the IPython session has a gui object.
Use the default Dock Area, available as gui.bec, unless you intentionally want a new window.

sections.heading: Check the Dock Area
sections.text:
The default Dock Area opened by Terminal + Dock is exposed as gui.bec.
gui.bec
If you want to create a separate Dock Area window instead, use:
dock_area = gui.new("my_dock_area")
For most interactive work, adding widgets to gui.bec is the simplest option.

sections.heading: List the available widgets
sections.text:
gui.available_widgets lists the widget classes that can be created from the command line.
gui.available_widgets
Common widget names include:
Waveform
ScanControl
Image
MotorMap
BECStatusBox
BECQueue
RingProgressBar

sections.heading: Add a dock
sections.text:
Widgets live inside docks. Create a dock first:
dock = gui.bec.new(name="live_plot")
The returned object is the dock. The dock name must be unique within the Dock Area.

sections.heading: Add a widget to the dock
sections.text:
Call new(...) on the dock to add a widget. The returned object is the widget.
waveform = dock.new(widget=gui.available_widgets.Waveform, name="samx_plot")
Assign the widget to a variable if you want to configure it afterwards:
waveform.plot(device_x=dev.samx, device_y=dev.bpm4i)
You can also pass the widget class name as a string:
waveform_from_string = dock.new(widget="Waveform", name="samx_plot_string")

sections.heading: Add a dock and widget in one command
sections.text:
For compact commands, BECDockArea.new(...) can create a dock and put a widget into it at the same time.
dock = gui.bec.new(
name="quick_plot",
widget=gui.available_widgets.Waveform,
widget_name="quick_waveform",
)
This form returns the dock, not the widget. Get the widget from the dock if you need to configure it:
waveform = dock.elements["quick_waveform"]
You can access the dock through the Dock Area:
gui.bec.quick_plot

sections.heading: Add another dock next to it
sections.text:
By default, new docks are added below the existing layout. Use position and relative_to when you want explicit placement.
scan_dock = gui.bec.new(
name="scan_control",
widget=gui.available_widgets.ScanControl,
position="right",
relative_to=gui.bec.live_plot,
)
Valid positions are:
bottom
top
left
right
above
below
You can still rearrange docks with the mouse after creating them.

sections.heading: Add a floating widget
sections.text:
Set floating=True to create the dock as a detached window.
status_dock = gui.bec.new(
name="status",
widget=gui.available_widgets.BECStatusBox,
floating=True,
)
To attach the floating dock again:
gui.bec.status.attach()

sections.heading: Put multiple widgets in one dock
sections.text:
Most GUI layouts use one widget per dock. If you need to place another widget into an existing dock, call new(...) on the dock itself.
dock = gui.bec.new(name="status_tools")
status = dock.new(widget=gui.available_widgets.BECStatusBox)
queue = dock.new(widget=gui.available_widgets.BECQueue, row=1, col=0)
Use row, col, rowspan, and colspan to place widgets inside the dock's grid layout.

sections.heading: Check the result
sections.text:
Inspect the Dock Area after adding widgets:
gui.bec.panels
Inspect widgets inside a dock:
gui.bec.live_plot.elements
Result
You added widgets to the BEC Dock Area from the IPython session and kept Python references for further configuration.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.text:
name identifies the dock, not the widget. Use widget_name if you also need a specific widget object name.
Dock names must be unique in one Dock Area.
relative_to should point to an existing dock, for example gui.bec.live_plot.
When controlling the GUI through RPC from IPython, use widgets listed in gui.available_widgets.

sections.heading: Next reading
sections.text:
Plot your first waveform
Create Your First GUI

pages.title: Add Widgets to a Dock Area
headings: Add Widgets to a Dock Area
Place a widget relative to another widget
Add a widget as a tab

sections.heading: Add Widgets to a Dock Area
sections.text:
Goal
Add BEC Widgets to an existing Dock Area from the BEC IPython client and control where they appear.
Use this guide when you already have BEC running with a Dock Area and want to add widgets with commands instead of the
toolbar. The examples use gui.bec, which is the default Dock Area in the Terminal + Dock layout.

sections.heading: Prerequisites
sections.text:
BEC is running with a Dock Area.
You are using the BEC IPython client.

sections.heading: Choose a widget
sections.text:
Available widget classes are exposed through gui.available_widgets. Use tab completion to inspect the available
widgets. In the BEC IPython client, type gui.available_widgets. and press the tab key.
gui.available_widgets
For example, Waveform, PositionerBox, and ScanControl can be created from the Dock Area:
gui.available_widgets.Waveform
gui.available_widgets.PositionerBox
gui.available_widgets.ScanControl

sections.heading: Add a widget
sections.text:
Use gui.bec.new(...) to add a widget to the Dock Area:
wf = gui.bec.new(gui.available_widgets.Waveform)
The returned object is the widget reference. Keep it in a variable when you want to configure it immediately:
wf.title = "bpm4i during samx scan"
wf.x_label = "samx"
wf.y_label = "bpm4i"

sections.heading: Place a widget relative to another widget
sections.text:
Use where and relative_to when the new widget should be placed next to an existing widget. In the BEC IPython
client, use the dock tab name as the reference:
pos = gui.bec.new(
gui.available_widgets.PositionerBox,
where="bottom",
relative_to="Waveform",
)
pos.set_positioner("samx")
where can be "left", "right", "top", or "bottom".
Add another widget to the right of the same Waveform:
wf2 = gui.bec.new(
gui.available_widgets.Waveform,
where="right",
relative_to="Waveform",
)
Use existing widget names
From the BEC IPython client, relative_to uses the name shown on the dock tab, for example "Waveform",
"ScanControl", or "PositionerBox".
If the same widget type appears multiple times, Dock Area indexes the repeated names. The first widget keeps the base
name, and later widgets use names such as "Waveform_0" and "Waveform_1".

sections.heading: Add a widget as a tab
sections.text:
Use tab_with when the new widget should share the same dock area as another widget:
wf_history = gui.bec.new(
gui.available_widgets.Waveform,
tab_with="Waveform",
)
wf_history.title = "History comparison"
You can tab more widgets with the same named dock:
scan = gui.bec.new(
gui.available_widgets.ScanControl,
tab_with="Waveform",
)

sections.heading: Inspect the Dock Area
sections.text:
List the BEC Widgets currently contained in the Dock Area:
gui.bec.widget_map()
gui.bec.widget_list()
Inspect the splitter layout when you need to understand how widgets are arranged:
gui.bec.describe_layout()

sections.heading: Remove widgets when needed
sections.text:
Remove one widget by dock name:
gui.bec.delete("Waveform_0")
Clear the full Dock Area:
gui.bec.delete_all()
Deleting widgets changes the current layout
If the current Dock Area profile is saved later, the saved profile will contain the updated layout. Save under a new
profile name when you want to keep the original layout.
Result
You added widgets to a Dock Area, placed them relative to existing widgets, created tabbed widgets, and inspected the
resulting layout from the BEC IPython client.

sections.heading: Related tasks
sections.text:
Use Plot Data using the IPython Client{ data-preview } when the widget you added
is a Waveform and you want to plot device data.
Use
Create Dock Area Profiles from the BEC IPython Client
when the layout should be saved as a reusable Dock Area profile.

pages.title: Plot Data using the IPython Client
headings: Plot Data using the IPython Client
Read plotted data back from the Waveform

sections.heading: Plot Data using the IPython Client
sections.text:
Goal
Create or reuse a Waveform widget from the BEC IPython client, plot device data, adjust plot and curve properties,
and retrieve plotted data.

sections.heading: Prerequisites
sections.text:
BEC is running with a Dock Area.
The samx and bpm4i devices are available in dev.
Device names
In these examples, samx is a simulated positioner motor and bpm4i is a
Beam Position Monitor.

sections.heading: Create a Waveform
sections.text:
Create a new Waveform in the default Dock Area:
wf = gui.bec.new(gui.available_widgets.Waveform)
If the profile already contains a Waveform, use the widget from the Dock Area namespace instead:
wf = gui.bec.Waveform

sections.heading: Plot device data
sections.text:
Plot bpm4i against the samx motor position:
wf.plot(device_x=dev.samx, device_y=dev.bpm4i)
Run a scan to produce live data:
scans.line_scan(dev.samx, -5, 5, steps=25, exp_time=0.1, relative=False)

sections.heading: Adjust the Waveform from IPython
sections.text:
The Waveform exposes plot properties through the same command interface:
wf.title = "bpm4i intensity during samx scan"
wf.x_label = "samx position"
wf.y_label = "bpm4i signal"
wf.x_grid = True
wf.y_grid = True
Curve items are also exposed below the Waveform when they are RPC-visible. Use get_curve(...) when you want an
explicit reference to a curve:
curve = wf.get_curve("bpm4i-bpm4i")
curve.set_color("#1f77b4")
curve.set_symbol("o")
curve.set_symbol_size(7)
curve.set_pen_width(2)
The same curve can usually also be reached through the Waveform namespace:
wf.bpm4i_bpm4i.set_color("red")
Discover available methods
Use tab completion on wf. or curve. to see exposed methods and properties. Use ? to inspect the docstring for
a method, for example wf.plot? or curve.set_color?.

sections.heading: Read plotted data back from the Waveform
sections.text:
The Waveform can also return the data that is currently plotted:
data = wf.get_all_data()
The result is a dictionary keyed by curve label:
data["bpm4i-bpm4i"]["x"]
data["bpm4i-bpm4i"]["y"]
Use this when you want to inspect a plotted curve, pass it to another Python package, or compare it with processed data.

sections.heading: GUI equivalent
sections.text:
You can configure the same device plot from the Waveform curve settings dialog:
Open the Waveform curve settings dialog from the plot toolbar :material-chart-timeline-variant:.
Set the x-axis mode to device.
Set the x-axis device to samx.
Add a y-axis curve for bpm4i.
Confirm the dialog and run the scan.
Result
The Waveform shows the device curve, and you can adjust the plot and curve properties from the BEC IPython client.

sections.heading: Related tasks
sections.text:
Use Fit Waveform Data with DAP
when you want to attach one or more DAP model curves to Waveform data.
Use Use Simulated Models from the IPython Client
to make bpm4i produce predictable simulated data.
Use Access History with a Waveform
to plot completed scans from history.
Use Script GUI Interactions
to combine BEC history access, Python analysis, and GUI plotting from a reusable function.

pages.title: Delete a Dock Area Profile
headings: Delete from the BEC IPython client

sections.heading: Delete a Dock Area Profile
sections.text:
Goal
Delete a locally created Dock Area profile from the Dock Area profile manager.

sections.heading: Prerequisites
sections.text:
You have BEC open with a Dock Area.
The profile you want to delete was created locally.
If you do not have profiles yet, first create one with
Save and Switch Dock Area Profiles{ data-preview }.
Read-only profiles from BEC Widgets or the beamline plugin repository cannot be deleted from the GUI.

sections.heading: Open the profile manager
sections.text:
Click the manage button :material-account-cog: in the Dock Area toolbar.
dock_area_toolbar_profile_manager.png

sections.heading: Select the profile
sections.text:
Click the profile you want to delete.
Check the metadata panel before deleting. Profiles from the local settings area can be deleted; bundled read-only
profiles cannot.
dock_area_manager.png
[Learn more about the profile manager fields](../../learn/gui/dock-area-profiles/profile-manager.md){ data-preview }
[Learn about Dock Area profile origins](../../learn/gui/dock-area-profiles/runtime-and-baseline-copies.md#profile-origins){ data-preview }
The profile origin controls whether the profile can be deleted from the profile manager.

sections.heading: Delete the profile
sections.text:
Click the delete button :material-trash-can-outline: .
Confirm the deletion when prompted.
Deleting a profile removes the writable copy from the local settings area.

sections.heading: Delete from the BEC IPython client
sections.text:
You can delete a local profile from the BECDockArea object in the BEC IPython client:
gui.bec.delete_profile("profile_name")
Replace profile_name with the name shown in the profile manager.
Result
The local profile is removed from the profile manager and no longer appears in the toolbar selector.

sections.heading: Common Pitfalls
sections.text:
The delete button is disabled for read-only profiles.
Deleting a local profile cannot be undone from the profile manager.
To make a useful profile available to other accounts, share it through the plugin repository before deleting your
local copy.

sections.heading: Dock Area Tasks
sections.text:
Use these guides when you need to add widgets to a Dock Area or manage Dock Area profiles.
If you are new to the Dock Area itself, start with
06 Create Your First GUI{ data-preview }. If you are
new to working with profiles, continue with
Dock Area Profiles{ data-preview }.

sections.heading: Choose the right task
sections.text:
Situation Use this guide What it changes
------------------------------------------------------------------ ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- -----------------------------------------------------------------------
You want to add another tool to the current Dock Area. Add Widgets to a Dock Area Creates a widget and places it in the current Dock Area.
You want to use a different saved layout now. Switch Dock Area Profiles Loads another profile into the current Dock Area.
The profile exists, but it is missing from the toolbar selector. Toggle Dock Area Profile Quick Selection Shows or hides the profile in the quick selector without deleting it.
The active profile has local layout changes you want to discard. Restore a Dock Area Profile to Its Baseline Replaces the runtime profile with its saved baseline.
A local profile is no longer useful. Delete a Dock Area Profile Removes the writable local profile from the profile manager.
Another e-account or beamline deployment needs the same profile. Share a Dock Area Profile with Other Accounts Copies the profile directly or adds it to the plugin repository.

sections.heading: Common Dock Area workflow
sections.text:
Most Dock Area work follows this order:
Create an initial Dock Area in
06 Create Your First GUI{ data-preview }.
Add widgets manually or with
BEC IPython commands{ data-preview }.
Save useful layouts as profiles with the
Dock Area Profiles
tutorial.
Switch between profiles{ data-preview } during normal work.
Adjust quick selection{ data-preview } so the toolbar only shows the
profiles you use often.
Restore a profile{ data-preview } when runtime changes should be discarded.
Share useful profiles{ data-preview } before deleting local copies.
The profile manager{ data-preview } is the safest place to
inspect profile metadata before changing or deleting a profile.

sections.heading: Learning material
sections.text:
Dock Area Profiles{ data-preview } explains what profiles are.
Runtime and Baseline Copies
explains profile storage, origins, and restore behavior.

pages.title: Fit Waveform Data with DAP
headings: Add a DAP curve to an existing curve
Initialize the curve with a fitting model

sections.heading: Fit Waveform Data with DAP
sections.text:
Goal
Attach DAP model curves to Waveform data from the BEC IPython client and inspect the fit output.
Use this guide when a Waveform already has a source curve, and you want to fit the curve and plot the fitted curve on
top. For basic Waveform
creation, plotting, and curve styling, start with
Control a Waveform from the IPython Client{ data-preview }.

sections.heading: Prerequisites
sections.text:
BEC is running with a Dock Area.
The samx and bpm4i devices are available in dev.
A Waveform source curve exists, or you are ready to create one.
Device names
In these examples, samx is a simulated positioner motor and bpm4i is a Beam Position Monitor.

sections.heading: Create a source curve
sections.text:
Create a Waveform and plot bpm4i against the samx motor position:
wf = gui.bec.new(gui.available_widgets.Waveform)
wf.plot(device_x=dev.samx, device_y=dev.bpm4i)
Run a scan to produce data:
scans.line_scan(dev.samx, -5, 5, steps=25, exp_time=0.1, relative=False)
The default source curve label is bpm4i-bpm4i, built from the y-axis device and signal.

sections.heading: Add a DAP curve to an existing curve
sections.text:
Attach a Gaussian Data Analysis Pipeline (DAP) to the existing bpm4i-bpm4i curve:
wf.add_dap_curve(device_label="bpm4i-bpm4i", dap_name="GaussianModel")
device_label is the existing source curve to fit. dap_name is the DAP model to attach to that source curve.

sections.heading: Initialize the curve with a fitting model
sections.text:
If you know in advance that your plot should also include a fit, add it in the initial plot call:
wf.plot(device_x=dev.samx, device_y=dev.bpm4i, dap="GaussianModel")
Do not call plot again with the same device pair after the source curve already exists. That creates a duplicate
source curve and raises an error. Use wf.add_dap_curve(...) to add a DAP model to an existing curve.

sections.heading: Use multiple DAP models
Inspect DAP output
sections.text:
Inspect the DAP result summary:
wf.get_dap_summary()
Inspect the fitted model parameters:
wf.get_dap_params()
DAP curves are also Waveform curve items. You can retrieve and style them in the same way as other curves:
fit_curve = wf.get_curve("bpm4i-bpm4i-GaussianModel")
fit_curve.set_color("orange")
fit_curve.set_pen_width(3)

sections.heading: GUI equivalent
sections.text:
You can configure the same DAP setup from the Waveform curve settings dialog:
Open the Waveform curve settings dialog from the plot toolbar :material-chart-timeline-variant:.
Set the x-axis mode to device.
Set the x-axis device to samx.
Add a y-axis curve for bpm4i.
Add the GaussianModel DAP model to the curve.
Confirm the dialog and run the scan.
waveform_fitting.gif
Result
The Waveform shows the source curve and the fitted DAP model curve, and you can inspect the fitted parameters from
the BEC IPython client.

pages.title: Plotting and Data Analysis from the BEC IPython Client
headings: Plotting and Data Analysis from the BEC IPython Client

sections.heading: Plotting and Data Analysis from the BEC IPython Client
sections.text:
Use these guides when you want to plot live data, inspect scan history, fit curves with DAP, or combine BEC Widgets
with ordinary Python analysis from the BEC IPython client.
If you are new to the gui object, read RPC GUI Control{ data-preview } for the
underlying command model. To create and switch Dock Area profiles from commands, use
Create Dock Area Profiles from the BEC IPython Client{ data-preview }.

sections.heading: Choose the right task
sections.text:
Situation Use this guide What it gives you
--- --- ---
You want to add a widget to the Dock Area before plotting. Add Widgets to a Dock Area Creates widgets and controls their dock placement from BEC IPython commands.
You want to plot live device data or style Waveform curves. Control a Waveform from the IPython Client Creates and configures Waveform plots from BEC IPython commands.
You want to attach DAP models to plotted data. Fit Waveform Data with DAP Adds one or more DAP model curves and reads fit parameters.
You want to inspect data from an already completed scan. Access History with a Waveform Plots history data in Waveform or reads raw values from bec.history.
You tried useful commands interactively and want to reuse them. Script GUI Interactions Turns plotting and light analysis steps into a small Python function.
You need predictable data for plotting or DAP examples. Use Simulated Models from the IPython Client Configures simulated device output before plotting it.

sections.heading: Common plotting workflow
sections.text:
Most command-line plotting work follows this order:
Configure a real or
simulated device signal{ data-preview }.
Add a widget to the Dock Area{ data-preview } when the layout does not already
contain the widget you need.
Plot live data in a Waveform{ data-preview }.
Add a DAP curve{ data-preview } when you need a fitted model.
Inspect scan history{ data-preview } when you need to compare with previous scans.
Read plotted data back from the Waveform with wf.get_all_data() for quick checks or small transformations.
Move repeated commands into a
small script{ data-preview } only after the
interactive workflow is useful.

sections.heading: Learning material
sections.text:
RPC GUI Control{ data-preview } explains how GUI command objects work.
GUI RPC Interface{ data-preview } lists common exposed methods.

pages.title: Restore a Dock Area Profile to Its Baseline
headings: Restore a Dock Area Profile to Its Baseline
Restore from the BEC IPython client

sections.heading: Restore a Dock Area Profile to Its Baseline
sections.text:
Goal
Replace the current runtime profile with its saved baseline profile.

sections.heading: Prerequisites
sections.text:
You have BEC open with a Dock Area.
The profile you want to restore is the active profile.
If you do not have profiles yet, first create one with
Dock Area Profiles{ data-preview }.

sections.heading: Activate the profile
sections.text:
Load the profile you want to restore.
Use Switch Dock Area Profiles if you need to activate a different profile first.

sections.heading: Start the restore action
sections.text:
Click the reset button :material-arrow-u-left-top: in the Dock Area toolbar.
restore_profile_toolbar.png
The Dock Area shows a confirmation dialog with previews of the current layout and the saved baseline layout.
restore_profile_dialog.png

sections.heading: Confirm the restore
sections.text:
Check the previews in the confirmation dialog.
Confirm the restore only if you want to replace the current runtime profile with the saved baseline profile.
When you confirm, BEC restores the runtime profile from the baseline profile and reloads the Dock Area.
[Learn about runtime and baseline profiles](../../learn/gui/dock-area-profiles/runtime-and-baseline-copies.md){ data-preview }
The Learn page explains how BEC stores runtime and baseline profiles, and why bundled profiles behave differently
from locally created profiles.
Result
The Dock Area uses the saved baseline layout for the restored profile.

sections.heading: Restore from the BEC IPython client
sections.text:
Use the IPython client when a script should restore a known baseline profile without opening the confirmation dialog:
gui.bec.restore_baseline_profile("alignment_cli", show_dialog=False)
Use Create Dock Area Profiles from the BEC IPython Client
for the introductory profile command workflow.

sections.heading: Common Pitfalls
sections.text:
Restoring a profile discards the current runtime profile for that profile.
For locally created profiles, saving again with the same name and confirming the overwrite updates the saved baseline
profile.
Profiles from the beamline plugin repository and profiles bundled with BEC Widgets are read-only; their bundled
baselines cannot be overwritten from the GUI.

pages.title: Share a Dock Area Profile with Other Accounts
headings: Share a Dock Area Profile with Other Accounts
Choose where to share the profile
Copy the profile into the plugin repository
Add the file to the plugin repository
Copy the profile to another e-account

sections.heading: Share a Dock Area Profile with Other Accounts
sections.text:
Goal
Find the .ini file for a locally saved Dock Area profile so you can share it with another e-account or add it to
the beamline plugin repository.

sections.heading: Prerequisites
sections.text:
You have saved and tested the profile locally.
You can access the e-account or beamline plugin repository where the profile should be copied.
You can open a Gitea pull request if the profile should become part of the plugin repository.
An e-account is the experiment account assigned to an experiment. It has limited storage access and owns the writable
Dock Area profile settings for that experiment.
[Learn how runtime and baseline profile copies are stored](../../learn/gui/dock-area-profiles/runtime-and-baseline-copies.md){ data-preview }

sections.heading: Find the saved profile
sections.text:
Open the profile manager from the Dock Area toolbar and select the profile.
Read the Runtime path field in the metadata panel. This is the editable .ini file for the saved profile.
Use this path as the source file when you copy the profile to another e-account or add the profile to the plugin
repository.
[Learn more about the profile manager fields](../../learn/gui/dock-area-profiles/profile-manager.md){ data-preview }

sections.heading: Choose where to share the profile
Copy the profile into the plugin repository
sections.text:
Copy the profile INI file into the preferred plugin repository profile directory:
/// tab :material-file-tree: Template path
/sls/ /config/bec/ / / /bec_widgets/profiles/
///
/// tab :material-map-marker-path: Example path
/sls/x01da/config/bec/production/debye_bec/debye_bec/bec_widgets/profiles/
///
Here, is the Git repository directory and is the Python package directory inside
that repository. In many beamline plugins they have the same name, for example debye_bec/debye_bec.
note
If the bec_widgets/profiles/ directory does not exist yet, create it before
copying the profile file.
Keep the file name readable and specific. For example:
alignment_scan.ini
The plugin repository path follows the same beamline repository layout described in
Add Changes to Your Plugin Repository{ data-preview }.

sections.heading: Add the file to the plugin repository
sections.text:
Continue with Add Changes to Your Plugin Repository to stage, commit, and
push the profile file.

sections.heading: Open a Gitea pull request
sections.text:
Open a pull request against the plugin repository's main branch.
After the pull request is approved and merged, the profile is available as a bundled profile when the next deployment
uses that commit.
///
/// tab :material-account-switch: Another e-account
Use this option for ad hoc sharing between two e-accounts. Copy the profile directly only when the profile does not need
to be reviewed, versioned, or distributed through the plugin repository.

sections.heading: Copy the profile to another e-account
Check the shared profile
sections.text:
After deployment or after copying the profile to another e-account, open BEC with a Dock Area.
Open the profile manager and verify that the profile is listed. Bundled profiles appear as read-only profiles and cannot
be overwritten or deleted from the GUI.

pages.title: Switch Dock Area Profiles
headings: Option 1: Switch from the quick selector
Option 2: Switch from the profile manager
Option 3: Switch from the BEC IPython client

sections.heading: Switch Dock Area Profiles
sections.text:
Goal
Load a saved Dock Area profile into the Dock Area.

sections.heading: Prerequisites
sections.text:
You have BEC open with a Dock Area.
The profile you want to load is already available.
If you do not have profiles yet, first create one with
Save and Switch Dock Area Profiles{ data-preview }.

sections.heading: Option 1: Switch from the quick selector
sections.text:
Use the quick selector when the profile is listed in the Dock Area toolbar. This is the shortest way to switch profiles.
Open the profile selector in the Dock Area toolbar and select the profile you want to load.
profile_switch.gif
The Dock Area loads the selected profile and replaces the current layout.
Quick selection
Not every profile is shown in the quick selector. A profile only appears there when quick selection is enabled for that
profile. Learn how to control this with Toggle Dock Area Profile Quick Selection{ data-preview }.

sections.heading: Option 2: Switch from the profile manager
Open the profile manager
sections.text:
Click the **manage button** :material-account-cog: in the Dock Area toolbar.
dock_area_toolbar_profile_manager.png

sections.heading: Select the profile
sections.text:
Click the profile you want to load.
Use the preview and metadata panel to confirm that you selected the correct profile.
dock_area_manager.png

sections.heading: Switch to the profile
sections.text:
Click the **switch profile button** :material-play-circle-outline:.
The selected profile is loaded into the Dock Area and replaces the current layout. The active profile is shown with the
filled green **switch profile button** icon :material-play-circle: .

sections.heading: Option 3: Switch from the BEC IPython client
sections.text:
Use the BEC IPython client when you want to load a profile from a command or script.
You can load the same profile from the BECDockArea object in the BEC IPython client:
gui.bec.load_profile("profile_name")
Replace profile_name with the name shown in the profile manager.
Result
The Dock Area now uses the layout saved in the selected profile.

sections.heading: Common Pitfalls
sections.text:
Switching profiles replaces the current Dock Area layout with the saved layout from the selected profile.
If the profile does not appear in the quick selector, open the profile manager and switch from there.
To make a profile appear in the quick selector, enable quick selection for that profile. Learn how to do that with
Toggle Dock Area Profile Quick Selection{ data-preview }.

sections.heading: Next Steps
sections.text:
Use Toggle Dock Area Profile Quick Selection{ data-preview } to control whether a profile appears
in the toolbar selector.
Use Restore a Dock Area Profile to Its Baseline{ data-preview } when you want to discard local layout
changes for the active profile.
Use Create Dock Area Profiles from the BEC IPython Client
when you want to create and load profiles from the IPython client.

pages.title: Toggle Dock Area Profile Quick Selection
headings: Toggle Dock Area Profile Quick Selection

sections.heading: Toggle Dock Area Profile Quick Selection
sections.text:
Goal
Show or hide a Dock Area profile in the Dock Area toolbar selector without deleting the profile.

sections.heading: Prerequisites
sections.text:
You have BEC open with a Dock Area.
The profile you want to change is already available.
If you do not have profiles yet, first create one with
Save and Switch Dock Area Profiles{ data-preview }.

sections.heading: Open the profile manager
sections.text:
Click the **manage button** :material-account-cog: in the Dock Area toolbar.
toolbar_profile_quick_select.png

sections.heading: Select the profile
sections.text:
Click the profile whose quick-select state you want to change.
Use the metadata panel to check the current quick-select state.
dock_area_manager.png
[Learn more about the profile manager fields](../../learn/gui/dock-area-profiles/profile-manager.md){ data-preview }

sections.heading: Toggle quick selection
sections.text:
Click the **toggle quick selection button** :material-star: .
If quick selection is enabled, the profile appears in the Dock Area toolbar selector. If quick selection is disabled,
the profile stays available in the profile manager but is hidden from the toolbar selector.
If you load a profile from the profile manager after disabling quick selection, the profile name can still appear in the
toolbar selector while that profile is active. After you switch to another profile, the disabled profile is removed from
the selector.

sections.heading: Check the toolbar selector
sections.text:
Close the profile manager or return to the Dock Area toolbar.
Open the **profile selector** and confirm that the profile is shown or hidden as expected.
Result
The profile remains available in the profile manager, and its visibility in the toolbar selector matches the
quick-select state you chose.

sections.heading: Common Pitfalls
sections.text:
Disabling quick selection does not delete the profile.
A hidden profile can still be loaded from the profile manager or BEC IPython Client.

sections.heading: Next Steps
sections.text:
Use Switch Dock Area Profiles{ data-preview } to load a profile from the manager.
Use Delete a Dock Area Profile{ data-preview } if you want to remove a local profile completely.
